title: He will sing over you (Zephaniah 3:17)
hookLine: God will rejoice over you with singing

cards: A parent at bedtime, the same song every night, slightly off key. A whole restaurant singing happy birthday while the guest of honor tries to hide under the table. A choir at a funeral.
Being sung to is strange and tender. The one being sung to does nothing; they just receive it. In church, the singing mostly goes one way: people sing to God.
Hymns, praise songs, chants. But tucked at the end of a short book full of warnings, the direction flips. There, it's God who sings.

teach.h: A BOOK THAT IS MOSTLY THUNDER.
teach.b: The book is Zephaniah, three short chapters set in the days of King Josiah. Most of it is thunder: warnings of the day of the LORD, a day of wrath, darkness and alarm.

A medieval Latin hymn about the last judgment, the Dies Irae, day of wrath, takes its opening words from Zephaniah's first chapter. So you'd expect the book to end in smoke. Instead, chapter three turns.
Sing, daughter of Zion. Shout. Be glad.
Then this, in the King James Bible: "The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing."
God isn't far off on a throne, but in the midst of thee, in the middle of the crowd, rejoicing over the people like a parent over a newborn, or a groom at a wedding.
The middle phrase is a puzzle: he will rest in his love.
The Hebrew can also be read as he will be silent in his love, or he will quiet you with his love. Translators differ. Maybe it's both: a love so deep it goes quiet, then breaks into song.
Some Christians choose this verse for baptisms and weddings, and some families paint it on a nursery wall.

teach.h: HE WILL JOY OVER THEE WITH SINGING.
teach.b: The God of the day of wrath, the book says, is also the God who sings over you.

how: Some churches read Zephaniah 3:14–20 during Advent, and some Christians choose verse 17 for baptisms, weddings and blessings over children.

o: day of joy: a Latin hymn sung at weddings
day of rest: the Latin name for the Sabbath
day of wrath: a Latin hymn drawn from Zephaniah

games.q: what's inside Zephaniah — tap the pairs.
p: a Latin hymn from chapter one
God in the middle of the people
or: be quiet in his love

s: the book of Zephaniah is mostly cheerful
most of it warns of the day of wrath. the joy comes at the end, in chapter three.
in Zephaniah 3:17, God is the one singing
"he will joy over thee with singing." the usual direction of worship flips.
everyone agrees on what "he will rest in his love" means
the Hebrew can also be read as silent in his love, or quieting you with love.

games.q: you've read two chapters of warnings about a day of wrath. what does Zephaniah say God will do at the end?
o: stay far away on a throne.
rejoice over the people with singing.
games.why: the book turns: God is in the midst of the people, and "will joy over thee with singing."

practice: Bring to mind someone you love, near or far, or someone gone, and picture them resting, safe. Then, very quietly, hum any tune over them, a lullaby, a hymn, a song from the car radio; you don't need words, or to sing well.
If you pray, hold them before God as you hum; if not, let the song carry your care.

wordCard.voice: Dies Irae. The medieval Latin hymn of judgment and wrath that borrows its opening words from Zephaniah, the same book that ends with God singing.

orig.note: Hebrew: a ringing cry of joy, a shout of song. the singing God does over the people.

carryVoice: Your line: sung over. You don't have to do a thing to be sung to. Until tomorrow.
